Activity.description:
First and last rating BY ON-CHAIN TIME, never by when we indexed it.

Both are null until the log scan backfills `block_time`, which is the
honest answer: we do not know yet. Substituting our own ingestion timestamp
would date every historical rating to the day of the backfill.

**`last_rating_at` is a COMPATIBILITY ALIAS as of 2026-09-10.** It means, and
will keep meaning for the life of v1, the last *eligible* rating — exactly
`freshness.last_eligible_rating_at`. It is not being renamed or corrected:
a client already reading it must keep reading the same thing. What it never
could answer — *was this subject described recently, whether or not it
counts?* — is what `freshness` adds next to it.

AgentScore.description:
One agent identity and EVERY rating it received.

The most detailed thing this API sells: not a number but the population
that produced it, row by row, with the transaction behind each one and the
revoked ones included. `caveats` comes BEFORE `ratings` on purpose — that
list can carry over 310,000 rows, and a warning that only shows up after it
is a warning nobody reads.

Everything else here is this response reading itself. **Advisory: it never moves the score and never fills a null one.** An empty list means no trap fired, NOT 'verified clean'. Caveat.description:
Una trampa que ESTOS números disparan, con su código estable.

🔴 `code` ES EL CONTRATO; `text` NO. El texto puede re-redactarse,
re-medirse o traducirse sin aviso — el código nunca cambia. Nace del hueco
H14 del 2026-08-28: los tres consumidores del ecosistema (Execution Market,
KarmaKadabra, MeshRelay) fueron instruidos ese mismo día de MOSTRAR estas
advertencias, y lo único que tenían para ramificar era la prosa. El texto ya
se había movido una vez (el corte de evidencia flaca, el 2026-08-25) y
cualquiera colgado de esa prosa se rompió ese día sin enterarse.

Se cambió la forma AHORA y no después a propósito: es el momento más barato
de la vida del proyecto para hacerlo — los tres consumidores están migrando
y ninguno construyó todavía contra la forma vieja. Dentro de dos semanas el
mismo cambio rompe tres integraciones vivas.

ChainStat.description:
El perfil de una cadena.

`avg_value` NUNCA viaja sola: `distinct_raters` y `top_rater_share` van al
lado en el mismo objeto, y esa es una decisión de producto, no de esquema.
Medido en este índice: avalanche promedia 76,95 y base 22,95, y el que lea
sólo esos dos números concluye que avalanche es mejor. La media de avalanche
sale de ONCE calificadores, con uno solo poniendo el 64 %; la de base, de
12.624. Publicar una media sin su N es el rumor que este sitio dice combatir.

El `example` del esquema es la fila REAL de solana leída del dominio el
2026-08-21 — no un payload inventado — y se eligió porque muestra el punto
de `stale_hours`: `blocks_behind` en 0 con casi ocho horas sin sincronizar.
La fila viva sale de `GET /chains`.

Concentration.description:
ADVISORY. Who the ratings came from. Never blocks, never moves a score.

Nullable ON PURPOSE, and consumers must handle the null: this is a
secondary aggregate, so when its query fails the endpoint drops the signal
rather than the answer. A reputation service that returns nothing because a
side-signal timed out has failed at its actual job.

`top_client_share` alone is not the tell. The campaign in this index — one
agent, 300.001 ratings, 57 raters, measured 2026-08-11 — sits near 0,14.
Read `distinct_raters` against `total_reviews`.

distinct_raters.description: **How many wallets spoke.** Read it against `total_reviews`: this is the pair that separates consensus from repetition, and it is the one that catches what share alone misses.
distinct_raters.title: Distinct Raters

top_client.description: Address of that loudest rater, so the claim can be checked.
top_client.title: Top Client

top_client_index_ratings.description: That rater's total live ratings across the whole index. Divided by `top_client_index_subjects` it gives what it leaves on a typical subject, and `top_client_ratings` against that mean is how hard it leaned on THIS one. **Read the two together, never the fan-out alone**: fan-out is a number an attacker controls end to end — rate a hundred subjects once each and a farm reads as a scanner. The pair is what `reading_policy.top_client_reach` and `top_client_burst` cut on, and it is published raw so you can redo the division instead of trusting ours. Null when there is no top rater.
top_client_index_ratings.title: Top Client Index Ratings

top_client_index_subjects.description: **That rater's fan-out: how many DISTINCT subjects it rates across the whole index**, not its volume here. This is the field that tells a farm from a sensor, and without it `top_client_share` cannot: an actor rating few subjects many times and a scanner sweeping the index both score high on share. Measured on the live index 2026-09-20: of the 43,711 subjects `top-client-share` marked, 42,278 (96.7%) had a top rater with fan-out over 100. Counted over live (non-revoked) ratings, which is a WIDER population than the one behind `top_client_share`: a rating this subject's score discards is still a subject that rater touched. Null when there is no top rater.
top_client_index_subjects.title: Top Client Index Subjects

top_client_ratings.title: Top Client Ratings

Confidence.description:
ADVISORY. How much evidence backs the number — never the number itself.

Nullable for exactly the same reason as `concentration`, and it goes null
with it: `distinct_raters` is read once, in SQL, and when that side query
degrades there is no N to band. A band invented over an N nobody could read
would be a label with no data under it.

`band == "no_ratings"` travels next to a **null** score, never a zero, and
`interval` is null there too: with no ratings the pure function returns the
whole domain (0-100) on purpose, but serialising a `lower: 0.0` beside a
null score would publish a 0 that is not a 0. Thresholds and policy version
ride along so the band can be reproduced without trusting a stale copy of
the cuts.

Freshness.description:
WHEN this subject was last described — the field this index was missing.

Two dates, because there are two questions and they have different answers:

* `last_received_feedback_at` — the last **real** NewFeedback in scope,
  whether or not it feeds the score. Revoked, out-of-domain and self-ratings
  included. Answers *"has anyone described this subject lately?"*.
* `last_eligible_rating_at` — the last rating that holds up **the number you
  are being shown**, under `policy_version`. Answers *"how old is THIS
  score?"*.

When the most recent rating was revoked the two differ, and the difference
IS the information: there was recent activity and the score does not
reflect it.

**Neither of them is `refreshed_at`**, which is when OUR materialised view
was recomputed and says nothing about the subject. A 2024 score inside a
view refreshed ten minutes ago looks new, and that reading is false — it is
the confusion this block exists to close.

Never rendered as "3 days ago" on our side: the relative text is derived
from UTC at the edge, because a cached SVG or a stored response would freeze
that phrasing forever.

dated_feedback_count.description: Received rows WITH an on-chain date. Half of the coverage denominator.
dated_feedback_count.title: Dated Feedback Count

eligible_dated_count.description: Same, over the ELIGIBLE subset — its own denominator, on purpose.
eligible_dated_count.title: Eligible Dated Count

eligible_timestamp_coverage.description: Coverage of the eligible subset. Separate from the one above because the two sets have different denominators, and a coverage without its denominator cannot be audited.
eligible_timestamp_coverage.title: Eligible Timestamp Coverage

eligible_undated_count.description: Eligible rows with no date yet.
eligible_undated_count.title: Eligible Undated Count

freshness_version.description: Version of the rules that produced this block — which rows count as received, which as eligible, how coverage is classified. Bumped when a rule moves, never when a date changes.
freshness_version.title: Freshness Version

indexer_checked_at.description: When we last looked at the chain for this scope — the upper bound of what we could possibly know. Across several chains it is the OLDEST check, not the newest: reporting the newest would turn 'we did not look' into 'nobody described them', which is the reassuring direction to be wrong in.
indexer_checked_at.title: Indexer Checked At

last_eligible_rating_at.description: Last rating that contributes to the score shown, same policy. Identical to `activity.last_rating_at` where both are served.
last_eligible_rating_at.title: Last Eligible Rating At

last_received_feedback_at.description: Last real NewFeedback in scope, by on-chain time. Revocation placeholders — rows we wrote for a `FeedbackRevoked` whose original we never indexed — are excluded: they are the shadow of a description, not a description.
last_received_feedback_at.title: Last Received Feedback At

refreshed_at.description: When the aggregate behind this row was recomputed. **Null when the answer came from the live grain** — there is no refresh to report, which is different from 'refreshed at epoch zero'. It is NOT when the subject was described.
refreshed_at.title: Refreshed At

timestamp_coverage.description: `none` (nothing received), `unknown` (received, none dated), `partial` (some dated) or `complete` (all dated), over `dated + undated`. `none` reads as 'no descriptions received' and never as 'date unknown' — no evidence and no date are different facts.
timestamp_coverage.title: Timestamp Coverage

undated_feedback_count.description: Received rows the log scan has not dated yet. The other half. Non-zero means the date above is a FLOOR: the real one may be newer.
undated_feedback_count.title: Undated Feedback Count

Health.description:
Liveness, index size and every policy in force — live, free and uncached.

🔴 **This route is the authority on every figure about this index.** No
total is typed by hand anywhere else in this API, on the site or in the
docs: indexing runs continuously, and a number written into a document goes
stale while still sounding exact. Ask here instead.

It is also where the effective value of every tunable parameter is
published, which is what keeps an environment override auditable rather
than an invisible drift.

agents.description: Agent identities indexed right now, across every chain. **Live and uncached** — this is the authoritative total, and the reason no page in this product types one.
agents.title: Agents

brigading.description: The brigading advisory — many DISTINCT wallets rating a subject once each in a short window, which is the OPPOSITE of what `top-client-share` and `campaign-per-rater` measure. `caveat_enabled: false` means the `brigading-suspected` caveat is never emitted; `jev_enabled: false` means the offline pass runs its SQL detector and calls no model. `threshold` is the cut on the probability of the coordinated-burst option — never on a model's confidence. **It never moves a score**: like every caveat, it is advisory text plus a suggested reading weight.
brigading.title: Brigading

build_sha.description: Git commit the running code was built from (stamped into the artifact at build time), or null when the build was not stamped.
build_sha.title: Build Sha

chains.description: One row per indexed chain, straight from the indexer's own sync state. Stable fields: `network` (the vocabulary for every `{network}` path parameter), `last_scanned_block`, `head_at_last_sync`, `started_at`, `updated_at` (when the last successful sync finished — the field that ages when a chain dies), and `last_error`. Chains scanned by signature instead of block number (solana) also carry `newest_signature`, `oldest_signature` and `backfill_complete`. Plus `next_sync_at`, computed here and not stored: `updated_at` plus `indexer_period_seconds`, or null when either is missing. A `next_sync_at` already in the past is not a bug — it means the tick that was due has not landed, which is exactly what you want it to say. For staleness measured against the clock, read `stale_hours` in `GET /chains`.
chains.title: Chains

confidence_policy.description: Version of the evidence bands. Names how much evidence backs a number without touching the number. **The four versions are separate because they change separately**: fusing them would mark every rating as recomputed each time a list is edited, and then the score's own version would stop meaning anything.
confidence_policy.title: Confidence Policy

confidence_thresholds.description: The distinct-rater cuts of each confidence band, here and free. This is what lets a consumer of the FREE `/leaderboard` — which already receives `distinct_raters` — derive the exact band without paying, and it is why the band is not repeated on every row: repeating a derivable string a hundred times adds bytes to a cached response, not a fact.
confidence_thresholds.title: Confidence Thresholds

credibility_m.description: M of the credibility weight per chain, Z = R / (R + M): the index's sigma²/tau² measured on production the day the policy was versioned (4.763 on 2026-09-04), frozen with `policy_version` rather than read live — a served score must not drift because the index grew. Published so every `per_chain[].weight` can be recomputed by hand.
credibility_m.title: Credibility M

feedback_entries.description: Individual ratings indexed right now — the grain everything else aggregates over. Live and uncached, same rule as `agents`.
feedback_entries.title: Feedback Entries

identity.description: Sign-in by signature (EIP-4361) for owners of ERC-8004 agents — the web app, not the API. `enabled: false` means the `/auth/*` and `/me/*` routes answer 404. Either way **no session ever reads a metered route**: payment stays the only authentication for reading. Also published: the domains and chain ids a signature is accepted for, the nonce and session lifetimes, the per-minute rate limits, and `erc1271_chain_ids` — the chains where a smart-account signature can be checked right now.
identity.title: Identity

indexer_period_seconds.description: How often the indexer runs, in seconds, as the running service has it configured — or null when the environment does not declare it. Null means unknown, never a guessed cadence.
indexer_period_seconds.title: Indexer Period Seconds

names.description: The on-chain name resolver behind `GET /names/resolve` and `GET /names/reverse`: the `uvd-describe-sdk` version, the naming systems it resolves, the per-lookup `timeout_seconds` and the cache lifetimes. Those routes run on their own Lambda function, so this block says what the code is, not the live state of that function. It never reads the index and never moves a score.
names.title: Names

ordering_policy.description: Version of how the leaderboard is ORDERED (Bayesian shrinkage). It never changes a published score — only the sort.
ordering_policy.title: Ordering Policy

policy_version.description: Version of the SCORE policy: credibility weight per chain (Z = raters / (raters + M)), value domain, revoked out, join by the identity's current owner. It is the one that travels in every scored response.
policy_version.title: Policy Version

rater_weight_policy.description: Version of the second weighting published beside every score as `weighted_score`. Advisory: it is not the served number.
rater_weight_policy.title: Rater Weight Policy

reading_policy.description: The **effective** cuts that fire a `caveats[]` entry, so a surface can READ them instead of typing them. This is the mechanism that keeps an environment override from being an invisible drift: the value actually in force is always legible here, free and without an account. Not a fifth policy and deliberately unversioned — it moves no score and no price. Left as a free-form object because its owner is the caveats module: a new cut has to reach whoever reads it without waiting for this file to catch up. A null inside IS data — `self_gap` is null because there is no self-rating threshold, the gap is always published.
reading_policy.title: Reading Policy

LeaderboardRow.description:
One row of the ranking, carrying the numbers that produced its position.

The row publishes BOTH scores and the N between them on purpose: a list
ordered by a number it does not show is a list you have to believe. With
these three fields the order can be recomputed by hand.

chain_count.description: How many chains contributed a score to this wallet.
chain_count.title: Chain Count

declared_types.description: The types declared by this wallet's identities. `null` is a legitimate member of the list: it means an identity that declares no type, which is common.
declared_types.title: Declared Types

distinct_raters.description: The N of that formula: **distinct raters, not ratings**, over the whole wallet. For a single-chain wallet (`chain_count == 1`) it recomputes `shrunk_score` by hand from this row alone; a multi-chain wallet needs the per-chain `score` and `distinct_raters` that `GET /reputation/wallet/{wallet}` publishes in `per_chain` — the order stays auditable, through two routes. It is also what lets a free caller derive the confidence band without paying — the cuts are in `GET /health`, which is why the band is not repeated on every row.
distinct_raters.title: Distinct Raters

final_score.description: The observed mean, untouched — the same number the paid wallet route serves. **It is not what decides the position.** Null, never 0, with no eligible ratings.
final_score.title: Final Score

networks.description: **Which** chains the wallet has a score on, not just how many. Without it a UI can say '3 chains' and not which — and one icon per network is the fastest way to read a profile that spans them.
networks.title: Networks

rank.description: Position in this ordering, 1-based. It comes from `shrunk_score`, not from `final_score`.
rank.title: Rank

shrunk_score.description: **What decides the position**: the Bayesian mean — each chain's observed score pulled toward the index prior by how many distinct raters back it ON THAT CHAIN, the shrunk chains then combined with the same credibility weights as `final_score` (two-level since 2026-09-04). Four glowing ratings cannot outrank four hundred, and a chain held by one person is pulled to the prior before it can vote. For a single-chain wallet it is exactly the one-level formula. Null when the index cannot form a prior.
shrunk_score.title: Shrunk Score

Ownership.description:
ADVISORY. What today's owner earned of this score, and what it inherited.

The split is the rating's `block_number` against the identity's
`owner_updated_block`: whatever landed before the handover was earned by
somebody else. It exists because without it a bought reputation — mint, get
rated, transfer — is indistinguishable from an earned one, and that is the
cheapest attack there is on an index like this one.

**It never moves `score`.** Both averages break down exactly the population
that produced `review_count`, which is why `inherited_review_count +
current_era_review_count + undetermined_review_count == review_count` adds
up by hand.

NULL MEANS "THE ERA CANNOT BE ESTABLISHED", NEVER "NOTHING WAS INHERITED".
It is null when there is no identity row, when `owner_updated_block` is
NULL, and **always on `solana`**: there that column is not the position of a
Transfer but the SLOT AT WHICH THE INDEXER READ the asset (ownership in
Metaplex Core is present state, not an event), so the predicate would flag
100,00 % of that chain's ratings as inherited — every single one. Publishing
that would accuse a whole network over a column-semantics bug.

AND IT IS NOT A VERDICT: a business sale, a custody migration or a wallet
rotation produce exactly the same figure as a bought reputation. The field
publishes counts and averages; the judgement is the reader's.

current_era_review_count.description: Eligible ratings SINCE the handover. 'Current era' means since the last transfer, not since the mint: no Transfer history is kept, so an identity that changed hands three times publishes one era.
current_era_review_count.title: Current Era Review Count

current_era_score.description: Mean over those. Null when there are none.
current_era_score.title: Current Era Score

identity_transferred.description: Whether the identity actually changed hands. **Not derivable from the counts**, which is why it travels: `inherited_review_count == 0` means two different things — the identity never moved, or it moved and nobody had rated it yet — and telling them apart is what this field is for. Null when no `Registered` row is indexed for it.
identity_transferred.title: Identity Transferred

inherited_review_count.description: Eligible ratings that landed BEFORE the handover.
inherited_review_count.title: Inherited Review Count

inherited_score.description: Mean over those. Null when there are none.
inherited_score.title: Inherited Score

inherited_share.description: Inherited fraction of the dated ratings, 0-1. Null with a zero denominator: a `0.0` would read as 'inherited nothing', which is a claim with no data behind it.
inherited_share.title: Inherited Share

owner_updated_block.description: The block the handover happened at — the line that splits the two eras. Every rating below it was earned by somebody else.
owner_updated_block.title: Owner Updated Block

undetermined_review_count.description: Eligible ratings the log scan has not dated yet, so neither era can claim them. **They are not distributed to either side** — guessing would be the cheap lie. This is why the three counts sum to `review_count` exactly.
undetermined_review_count.title: Undetermined Review Count

Deliberately: ranking raters would be a NEW verdict ("this publisher is
trustworthy"), and this index returns evidence, not verdicts. You get the
activity decomposed -- volume, distinct subjects, dispersion,
concentration, roles -- and YOU decide what it means.

distinct_subjects.description: How many different agents it rated. Read against `ratings_emitted`: a big ratio is a rater talking about the whole index, a small one is a rater talking about one thing.

value_stddev.description: Dispersion of those values. **A rater stamping the same number on everything has stddev 0** — we surface it, we do not verdict it. Null when there is nothing to disperse.

Rating.description:
One individual rating, exactly as it was written on chain.

This is the grain of the whole index — every score in this API is an
aggregate over rows of this shape, and the paid agent route returns them
one by one, revoked ones included, each with the transaction that proves
it. A revocation nobody can audit is not a revocation.

author_class.description: Who signed this row, as a class. `facilitator-authored`: `client` is a known relayer (today the x402 facilitator's EVM wallet) that wrote the rating on behalf of the real rater, so `client` is NOT the counterparty — every such row shares one `client`, and any per-rater count merges them into one. `rater-authored`: `client` is not a relayer this index knows about; it does not prove who signed. Per rating only: no score or aggregate is computed by author class.
author_class.title: Author Class

block_number.description: Block the rating landed in. Null until the log scan dates it.
block_number.title: Block Number

block_time.description: Time of the block containing the feedback event. Distinct from the interaction time claimed inside its document and the retrieval time.
block_time.title: Block Time

client.description: Who wrote this rating: the rater's address. This is the field the whole product is about — a score without its raters is a rumor.
client.title: Client

document.description: Feedback document retrieval, integrity and parser status. Null until queued or when no URI exists. Succeeded means processing finished, not verified claims: read integrity_state separately. Content and human observations require separate authorization.

endpoint.description: Endpoint declared in the original feedback event, unchanged and unverified.
endpoint.title: Endpoint

feedback_hash.description: Content hash the rater committed to, when it declared one.
feedback_hash.title: Feedback Hash

feedback_index.description: The rater's own counter for this subject, part of the natural key `(network, agent_id, client, feedback_index)`. It is what makes re-indexing idempotent.
feedback_index.title: Feedback Index

feedback_uri.description: The `feedbackURI` the standard carries — where the rater published the rating. The three `issuer*` fields below are read from it.
feedback_uri.title: Feedback Uri

is_revoked.description: The rater took this rating back. Excluded from every score, returned anyway — with `revoked_tx` — because a revocation nobody can audit is not a revocation.
is_revoked.title: Is Revoked

is_self.description: The rater IS the rated agent's current owner. Attribution, not eligibility: it travels on every row — revoked and out-of-domain included — so the breakdown says where each point came from without the caller recomputing the comparison. Self-ratings are out of every score and summarised in `self_rated`.
is_self.title: Is Self

issuer.description: Canonical name of the issuing product when the host is a known Ultravioleta DAO service (e.g. `execution-market`), else null. Null does NOT mean unknown issuer — read `issuer_host` for that.
issuer.title: Issuer

issuer_attribution.description: Independent operator-reviewed attribution from the event network, client and block interval, with evidence source. Never inferred from IPFS gateway or issuer claims inside the document. Null when no unambiguous verified binding exists.
issuer_attribution.title: Issuer Attribution

issuer_host.description: Host of `feedback_uri`, lowercased and without `www.` — where this rating was published. Null when the rating carries no http(s) URI. Present for ~82% of the index.
issuer_host.title: Issuer Host

issuer_org.description: `uvd` when this rating was written by an Ultravioleta DAO product, else null. One stable label, independent of how many products there are or what each is called.
issuer_org.title: Issuer Org

log_index.description: Position within the block. Null until the log scan dates it.
log_index.title: Log Index

normalized_value.description: `value` brought to the 0-100 domain — the only figure comparable across emitters. Null when the row is out of domain, which is also why it was excluded from the score.
normalized_value.title: Normalized Value

revoked_tx.description: The transaction that killed this rating. Without it a revocation is unauditable — which is why it travels instead of the row simply disappearing.
revoked_tx.title: Revoked Tx

tag1.description: The rater's first tag: the AREA being judged (`trust`, `liveness`, `contractRisk`, `activity`, …) and, when the emitter declares it, the direction prefix. This is what `facets` are keyed by. Free vocabulary — the index carries hundreds of distinct values, so read it, never split it on `:` and hope.

tag2.description: The rater's second tag, if any.

tx_hash.description: The transaction that wrote this rating — go verify it in an explorer, which is the point. **Null until the log scan reaches this entry**, not null forever.
tx_hash.title: Tx Hash

value.description: The raw on-chain integer, untouched. Read it together with `value_decimals`; use `normalized_value` for anything comparable.

SearchMatch.description:
Una fila que el índice reconoció, con la LECTURA bajo la cual la encontró.

`interpreted_as` viaja por fila y no en la raíz porque un mismo string
base58 puede ser wallet Y asset a la vez: `wallet_chains` lo toma como
wallet de Solana y `agent_reputation` lo toma como asset de Metaplex Core —
dos sujetos distintos, con dueños distintos, escritos igual. Fundir las dos
lecturas en una etiqueta de raíz borraría cuál produjo cuál.
SearchMatch.title: SearchMatch

SearchResult.description:
Lo que la caja entendió y dónde lo encontró, en dos capas separadas.

La separación ES el diseño: `interpretations` (raíz) es lo que la **forma**
permite —léxico, barato, no toca la base—, y `matches[].interpreted_as` es
bajo qué lectura el **índice** encontró esa fila. Una entrada puede tener dos
interpretaciones y cero matches, o una interpretación y once matches.

**No existe el valor `"ambiguous"` y no hay un `ambiguous: bool`.** La señal
de ambigüedad es `len(interpretations) > 1`, que además dice CUÁLES son;
colapsarlas en una etiqueta borra esa información, que es el modo de falla
que este repo persigue.

El `example` del esquema es una respuesta REAL, leída del índice el
2026-08-23 — no una maqueta. Es un base58 de Solana a propósito: la forma
admite dos lecturas (`interpretations` trae dos) y el índice sólo encontró
filas bajo una (`matches` trae una, `interpreted_as: solana_asset`), y ese
desfase entre las dos capas es justamente lo que un ejemplo con una sola
interpretación no muestra. Su `refreshed_at` en `null` también es real: esta
fila salió del grano vivo, no de una vista materializada.

matches.description: What the index knows under that string. An empty list with a non-empty `interpretations` means the shape was valid and nothing matched — not that the query was wrong.
matches.title: Matches

normalized_query.description: What we actually looked up. It differs from `query` only for EVM input, which is lowercased; a base58 travels byte for byte, because lowercasing it would silently invent a different key.
normalized_query.title: Normalized Query

query.description: Exactly what you sent, untouched. It is the only thing that lets you see you pasted a trailing space or an invisible character.
query.title: Query

SearchResult.title: SearchResult

SelfRated.description:
Lo que el sujeto dice de si mismo — excluido del score, no del perfil.

`gap` = self - others. Positivo significa que se sobrevalora. Es la lectura
mas informativa del perfil y sale gratis del predicado que ya excluye la
autocalificacion del promedio.

It exists so a decision made on this data can be re-read later and

El `example` del esquema es la respuesta REAL del dominio para la wallet

A quality gate built on this route must treat every code listed here as unverified, not as passed.

WalletScore.description:
One wallet's reputation, decomposed into what produced it.

The headline number is `final_score`, but it is the least interesting field
here: everything beside it exists so the number can be checked instead of
believed — which chains it came from, which areas disagree, how many
distinct counterparties are behind it, and what the subject says about
itself.

activity.description: First and last rating **by on-chain time**, never by when we indexed the row.

caveats.description: The traps THESE numbers trigger, already written out. Derived from the fields of this same response — `final_score`, `total_reviews`, `concentration`, `self_rated` — never from a second query, which is why it costs nothing extra. **Advisory: it never moves the score and never fills a null one.** An empty list means no trap fired, NOT 'verified clean'. Each entry is `{code, text}`: branch on `code`, which is permanent; `text` is Spanish prose meant to be shown to whoever is deciding and may be rewritten or re-measured without notice. Same objects the MCP tool `describe_lookup_wallet` returns: one policy, two doors.
caveats.title: Caveats

chain_count.description: How many chains contributed a score — how many terms the weighted mean above has, not how many chains the wallet merely appears on.
chain_count.title: Chain Count

concentration.description: ADVISORY, and **nullable on purpose**: this is a secondary aggregate, so when its query degrades the endpoint drops the signal rather than the answer. Never moves a score.

confidence.description: ADVISORY band over how much evidence backs the number — never the number itself. Goes null together with `concentration`, and for the same reason: the band is computed over `distinct_raters`, and a band invented over an N nobody could read would be a label with no data under it.

facets.description: Reputation by area, keyed by the rater's `tag1` — `trust`, `liveness`, `contractRisk` and `activity` are separate judgements, not a mean. **Ordered by volume desc**: dict order is the ranking, so a client can take the first N without re-sorting. The overall score and one facet can disagree by more than 30 points on the same wallet, and that gap is the product.
facets.title: Facets

final_score.description: The published score, 0-100: the **credibility-weighted mean of the per-chain scores** — Σ weight_k·score_k / Σ weight_k over `per_chain`, weight_k = distinct_raters_k / (distinct_raters_k + M). A chain carrying hundreds of thousands of ratings cannot drown one carrying forty people, and one rater on a spare chain weighs 0.174 — never half the wallet, which is what equal weight allowed until 2026-09-04 (one signature moved a 220-rating wallet by 17 points). Revoked, out-of-domain and self-ratings are out of it. **Null, never 0**, when there is no eligible rating: no data is not bad data.
final_score.title: Final Score

per_chain.description: The score per chain, never collapsed — keyed by network, each with its `distinct_raters` and its `weight`. This is the breakdown `final_score` is made of, so the number can be recomputed by hand.
per_chain.title: Per Chain

policy_version.description: The aggregation policy that produced these numbers. It travels in every scored response so two callers can never be served different numbers without the difference being visible, and so a stored number can be traced back to the rules that made it.
policy_version.title: Policy Version

rater_weight_policy.description: Version string of the weighting that produced `weighted_score`. Also published free in `GET /health`.
rater_weight_policy.title: Rater Weight Policy

self_rated.description: What the subject said about itself — excluded from every score above, published here instead of hidden. `gap = self - others`: positive means it overrates itself.

snapshot.description: Only on `?snapshot=true`: the durable receipt row that was written, with its `inputs_digest` and `policy_version` — something you can hand a counterparty and we can recompute identically. Null on a plain read, which writes nothing.

total_reviews.description: Eligible ratings behind the score, summed across chains. Read it against `concentration.distinct_raters`: the two together are what separates consensus from repetition.
total_reviews.title: Total Reviews

wallet.description: The subject, echoed back as it was resolved. EVM addresses come back lowercased (the grain guarantees it); Solana base58 ids keep their case, because there case IS identity.
wallet.title: Wallet

weighted_score.description: The SAME grain under a second weighting (`rater_weight_policy`), published beside the served number rather than replacing it. **It is not the policy**: `final_score` is what this API serves and what a snapshot records. It travels because changing how hundreds of thousands of ratings are weighted is not something a reputation index gets to do silently. Null means two different things and `final_score` tells them apart: if that one has a number and this one does not, the side signal degraded; if both are null, the wallet has no evidence.
weighted_score.title: Weighted Score

x402.description:
**Payment is the authentication.** There is no account, no API key and nothing to register: the credential for a metered call is a base64 x402 payload carrying an EIP-3009 USDC authorization that YOU sign locally — no private key ever leaves your side.

How to get one: call the operation with no header at all. It answers **402** with the challenge (asking is free and is the intended first move), you sign `accepts[]` — the only thing you sign against — and you replay the identical request with this header. The 200 comes back with `X-Payment-Receipt`.

Two properties no `apiKey` scheme can express, so read them here: the credential is **per call** (the nonce is consumed at settlement, so it will not pay twice) and a receipt is reusable only for the byte-identical resource — wallet A's receipt cannot unlock wallet B. Full contract: https://describe.net/auth.md

info.description:
## A score without its raters is a rumor.

**describe.net decomposes any ERC-8004 reputation into the counterparties that wrote it: how many they are, how many times each one spoke, on what, and when.**

Built for agents that have to vet a counterparty before they sign — one HTTP call instead of hours of archive RPC across chains. No account, no API key, no token: the free tier answers without headers, and the metered tier is paid per call with x402 over USDC. **Payment is the authentication.**

**How big is the index? Ask it: `GET /health`** — agents, individual ratings and how far the scan reached on each chain, live, free and uncached. The numbers are not repeated on this page on purpose: indexing runs continuously, and a total typed into a document is a total that goes stale while still sounding exact.

Scoring policy `credibility-weight-per-chain@1` · ranking `bayes-shrinkage-two-level@3` · published rater weighting `one-voice-per-counterparty+bounded-trust@1` · evidence bands `wilson-raters@1`. Every scored response carries its `policy_version`: two callers can never be served different numbers.

### Rate limits

Throttling happens at the edge (API Gateway), per route key, and above the budget the gateway answers **HTTP 429** before the request reaches the application — back off and retry; a second of pause clears the bucket. **This build was not told the gateway's numbers, so it does not print them here**: read `RateLimit-Policy` on any response (RFC 9239 syntax, requests per 1-second window plus the burst), which is read from the gateway's own configuration and is therefore the authority. A per-request `RateLimit` counter (remaining/reset) is **not** emitted on purpose: the application does not see the gateway's budget, and a fabricated counter is worse than none. Cached free routes (`/health`, `/pricing`, `/leaderboard`, `/stats/*`) are served by CloudFront and do not consume the budget on a cache hit.

**`GET /wallets/{wallet}/exists` has its own, lower budget** (also under `/v1`), and this build was not told its numbers: read `RateLimit-Policy` on its responses.

**The name routes (`GET /names/resolve`, `GET /names/reverse`) share their own, much lower budget** (also under `/v1`), and this build was not told its numbers: read `RateLimit-Policy` on their responses.

### Versioning & deprecation

The API is versioned by this document's `info.version` (semver), not by URL paths. The `/v1` prefix is an alias of the very same contract, not a second version of it; every route is the current contract. **A breaking change to a served field bumps the major version and ships with a new `API_VERSION`, never silently**: that is the standing rule this repo already applies (a field changing *type* counts as breaking, a new optional field does not). Scored numbers are versioned separately and per-response via `policy_version` — if the scoring policy changes, that string changes with it, so any cached or stored number can be traced to the policy that produced it. Deprecations are announced in this description and in [llms.txt](https://describe.net/llms.txt) before removal; there is no fixed sunset window to cite yet, and this page will say so when one exists rather than inventing one here.

### Features

| Feature | What it means |
|---|---|
| Cross-chain ERC-8004 index | One row per individual rating, scanned from `Registered` and `NewFeedback` logs and joined to the agent's **current** owner — never the minter, which is usually the facilitator that minted the id before transferring it. |
| Credibility weight per chain | A wallet's score is the credibility-weighted mean of its per-chain scores: each chain votes with `distinct_raters / (distinct_raters + M)`, so a chain carrying hundreds of thousands of ratings cannot drown one carrying forty people, and one rater on a spare chain weighs 0.174 — never half the wallet. Inherited from DescribeMe's Bayesian ranking. The per-chain detail ships in `per_chain` with each chain's raters and weight, never collapsed. |
| Bayesian shrinkage in the ranking | The leaderboard is ordered by `shrunk_score` — the observed mean pulled toward the index prior by how many **distinct raters** back it. Both numbers and that N travel in every row, so the order can be recomputed by hand instead of believed. |
| Self-ratings excluded, not hidden | A subject rating itself is out of every score and published separately as `self_rated`, with `gap = self - others`. Positive means it overrates itself. |
| Facets by tag | The rater's `tag1` kept apart — `trust`, `liveness`, `contractRisk`, `activity` are separate judgements, not a mean. The overall score and one facet can disagree by more than 30 points on the same wallet; that gap is the product. |
| Concentration signal | `distinct_raters`, `top_client_share` and `top_client` on every profile. Advisory — it never moves a score. Read `distinct_raters` against `total_reviews`: the largest campaign in this index sits **under 0.15 on share**, so any threshold on share alone waves it through. What gives it away is thousands of ratings per distinct rater. Verify the campaign for free — `miner-vouch` in `GET /stats/facets` carries over 310,000 ratings with `distinct_agents: 1`, against the index total in `GET /health`. |
| Provenance per rating | Agent detail returns every rating with its `tx_hash`, block number and log index — revoked ones included, with the transaction that killed them. A revocation nobody can audit is not a revocation. |
| Time series on on-chain time | History buckets by the **block** timestamp, never by when we indexed the row, and reports `coverage.undated_reviews` so a series shorter than the score reads as coverage rather than as a bug. |
| Second weighting published alongside | `weighted_score` and `rater_weight_policy` travel next to `final_score`. Changing how hundreds of thousands of ratings are weighted is not something a reputation index gets to do silently. |
| Citable snapshot | `?snapshot=true` persists a durable row with `inputs_digest` + `policy_version`: a receipt you can hand a counterparty and we can recompute identically. |
| MCP server | The same index as thirteen tools inside your MCP client: five are priced like the routes behind them, the other eight never charge. |

### Pricing

One rule decides the line, and it is a rule about cost: **free is what a cache serves everybody; charged is what only you asked for.** The aggregate view of the index is free forever. The question about *your* counterparty is what costs money, which is exactly when the answer is worth something.

**Free — HTTP 200, no headers, no account.** Start here: reading the free tier costs nothing and tells you whether the metered tier is worth it.

| Route | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| `GET /health` | Liveness, plus how far the scan reached on each chain and the four policy versions in force. |
| `GET /pricing` | Every price, machine-readable, each with the reason it costs that. The only route that never touches Postgres. |
| `GET /docs` · `/redoc` · `/openapi.json` | **The live schema** — what this build is serving at this instant, rendered two ways. The written documentation (a guide for every door, plus this schema sealed with its date so you can cite it) is at [docs.describe.net](https://docs.describe.net/). |
| `/a2a/?` | — |
| `/mcp/?` | — |
| `/api/?` | — |
| `/\.well-known/.*` | — |

Pricing table `cost-tiered@10`, served machine-readable and free at `GET /pricing`, each price with the reason it costs that. **The authoritative price for one call is the `accepts[]` array of that call's own 402** — the price can depend on the parameters, which a table per route cannot express.

### How to pay

Five steps, no registration, nothing to do before your first call. If you can sign an EIP-3009 authorization you are already a customer.

1. **Call the route you want. Do not pre-authorize.** Asking without paying is free and is the intended first move — the 402 is a price quote, not an error.
2. **Read the challenge.** The 402 body carries `amount`, `resource`, `recipient`, the pricing tier with its reason, and `accepts[]` — one entry per network. **`accepts[]` is the only thing you sign against.** Its `amount` is in token base units (USDC has 6 decimals, so `"10000"` is $0.01); the top-level `amount` is the human dollar figure and must not be signed. Take the USDC contract from `accepts[].asset`, never from a document.
3. **Check who you are about to pay, every time.** The only address describe.net will ever ask you to pay is `0xe4dc963c56979E0260fc146b87eE24F18220e545`, published here and pinned out of band in the MCP server and in `auth.md`. If `payTo` differs, **do not pay** — either the challenge did not come from us, or the treasury changed and this page is stale. Both are resolved by asking, not by signing.
4. **Sign an EIP-3009 `TransferWithAuthorization`** for that `amount`, to that `payTo`, for that `asset`, on that network, and base64-encode the x402 payload. You sign locally and send a signature — no private key ever leaves your side. An MCP wallet (`ows_sign_eip3009`, `pay_x402`) or `uvd-x402-sdk` will produce the string for you.
5. **Replay the identical request with the `X-PAYMENT` header.** Same method, same path, same query string, one header more. Payment is verified and settled on-chain **before** the query runs; the 200 comes back with `X-Payment-Receipt` (the settlement transaction hash — public, keep it to reconcile) and `X-Payment-Reused`.

Networks the challenge will offer, chosen by settlement gas rather than by price — we pay the gas, and paying L1 gas to collect one cent would be selling at a loss:

| Network | Chain ID |
|---|---|
| `base` | 8453 |
| `avalanche` | 43114 |
| `arbitrum` | 42161 |
| `optimism` | 10 |
| `polygon` | 137 |
| `celo` | 42220 |

**Three rules that save money.** One authorization per paid call: the nonce is consumed at settlement, so a credential that already paid will not pay again. A receipt is reusable, but only for the byte-identical resource — wallet A's receipt cannot unlock wallet B, and the reused read answers `X-Payment-Reused: true`. And **a 503 is not a 402**: `facilitator_unavailable` means your authorization was NOT used, so retry the same request with the *same* `X-PAYMENT` after `Retry-After` — signing a fresh one there can make you pay twice. Full flow, with worked examples: https://describe.net/auth.md

### What we do NOT do

| Not this | Why it matters to you |
|---|---|
| Not a block explorer | No balances, no transactions, no contract state. We serve the ratings; each one carries its `tx_hash` so you can go verify it in an explorer, which is the point. |
| Not a price oracle | No token prices, no TVL, no market data. The only dollar figures here are our own prices. |
| Not a credit score | Nothing here predicts default and nothing here is an approval. We report who rated a subject, how many of them there were, on what, and when. The decision stays yours — and a single number was never enough to make it. |
| Not a writer to any chain | Zero contracts deployed, zero transactions signed by us. This is a read-only index; the only thing that moves on-chain is your own payment, settled by the facilitator. |
| Not an identity service | A wallet is a wallet. There is no name lookup and no person search, and no amount of on-chain behaviour makes us call a subject a person. |

**A feed of facts, not of opinions.** Every row already happened in a finalised block and is already public: who rated which identity, with what value, under which facet, and in which transaction. Ordered by `block_time`, the chain's own clock, never by when we indexed it: this index backfilled years of history in one afternoon, so ordering by our clock would pile the whole past onto that day.

Same validity domain as every score on this site: revoked ratings are out, and so is anything outside `0 < value <= 100`. A feed that showed what the score discards would teach you a reality no other endpoint confirms.

With it the planner enters by the chain and reads an already-ordered index — `limit` rows and stop. Avalanche measured 26.711 ms → 3.058 ms (new disk, no index) → 0,77 ms (with the index). The evidence itself, not a summary of it: every individual rating with its `tx_hash`, block number and log index, so each one can be checked in an explorer. **Revoked ratings included**, each with the transaction that killed it — a revocation nobody can audit is not a revocation.

`score` applies the full policy — revoked out, domain 0 < v ≤ 100, no self-rating — and what it excludes stays listed and counted: `out_of_domain_count`, `self_rated` with its gap, and `is_self` on every row, so `review_count + revoked_count + out_of_domain_count + self_rated.count` always equals the length of `ratings`.

**That same arithmetic now holds inside each facet**: `count + revoked_count + out_of_domain_count + self_rated_count` is every row that carried that tag, under the same precedence (revoked > out-of-domain > self). It does NOT have to add up to the totals above: a facet whose ratings were all discarded is not listed at all, so the per-facet discards can sum to LESS than the agent-level ones. Each facet also carries `distinct_raters`, how many spoke rather than how many times; it is advisory and **must not be added across facets** (one rater who judged two areas counts in both, so the agent's total stays `concentration.distinct_raters`).

`ownership` splits that same population in two by ON-CHAIN POSITION: the ratings that landed **before** the current owner took the identity (`inherited_*`) and the ones it earned itself (`current_era_*`), plus the ones the log scan has not placed yet (`undetermined_review_count`). The three counts add up to `review_count`, and it is **advisory: it never moves `score` and never fills a null one**. get.description:
**The core product.** Everything that produced the score, not just the score: `per_chain` (never collapsed), `facets` by the rater's tag — each one with `distinct_raters` and what it threw away (`revoked_count`, `out_of_domain_count`, `self_rated_count`) — `self_rated` with its `gap`, `concentration` (`distinct_raters`, `top_client_share`, `top_client`), `confidence` (the named evidence band, its Wilson interval, the thresholds and what to do about it), `activity` by on-chain time, `caveats` (the traps these particular numbers trigger, already written out), and both `final_score` and `weighted_score` side by side with the policy that produced each.

`caveats` costs nothing extra — it is derived from the fields above, not from a second query — and it is the same list the MCP tool returns, from the same module. An empty array means no trap fired, not 'verified clean'.

`confidence` is **advisory**: it never moves the score and never fills a null one. When the band is `low`, treat the point value as no evidence and decide on the interval — the same instruction QuickNode publishes for its own confidence tier.

A wallet we have no evidence about is a **200 with a null score**, not a 404: *we hold nothing on this counterparty* is a useful answer to someone deciding whether to sign.

Inside a facet, `distinct_raters` is **how many spoke**, not how many times: hundreds of thousands of ratings from a few dozen raters and a few thousand from thousands of raters look identical as `{score, count}` and are not the same evidence. The free `GET /stats/facets` publishes, live, how many ratings and how many distinct agents every facet in this index carries. **Do not add `distinct_raters` across facets** — one rater who judged two areas counts in both; the subject's total is `concentration.distinct_raters`. The three discard counters are advisory and mutually exclusive (revoked > out-of-domain > self), so per facet `count + revoked_count + out_of_domain_count + self_rated_count` is every row that carried that tag. A facet whose ratings were **all** discarded is not listed at all.

`concentration` may come back null on its own while the rest of the answer stands — a side signal that timed out must not take the answer with it. `confidence` follows `concentration`: its N is read once, in SQL, so when that signal degrades both come back null. Handle the null.

get.description:
**Paste what you have.** An EVM address, a Solana base58 id, or an ERC-8004 agent id — the answer says what it was read as and where it exists, one row per chain, each with the wallet that owns it **there**.

Free for the same reason `GET /wallets/{wallet}/chains` is: this is the number and the location, never the decomposition. Who rated, how many times, in what facet, on what date and in which transaction stays paid at `GET /reputation/wallet/{wallet}` and `GET /reputation/agent/{network}/{agent_id}` — and every row here carries the exact route for its own subject in `detail_route`. Charging for this would also mean billing your typos: the paywall runs before any validation.

**Two layers, and the split is the point.** `interpretations` at the root is what the *shape* allows; `matches[].interpreted_as` is the reading under which the *index* found that row. A base58 string can be a wallet **and** a Metaplex Core asset at once, and those are different subjects with different owners — so both readings are answered and both are labelled. **Ambiguity is `interpretations` having more than one entry**; there is no `"ambiguous"` value, because a single label erases *which* readings were possible.

The same numeric id is a different agent on every chain: an id that exists on three chains answers with three rows, three owners and three scores. A chain where the identity exists but nobody rated it answers `final_score: null` — registered and unrated is not the same as absent.

**Exact match only** — no prefix, no wildcard, no listing, no paging. You get back what you already knew how to name. And an input we have never seen is a **200 with `matches: []`**, never a 404: a 404 here would claim the registry has no such entry, and a loose string names no entry to be missing.

get.description:
**The number, free.** Which ERC-8004 identities a wallet holds on each chain, and the reputation it accumulated there — scored with that chain's ratings only.

This is free on purpose, and the reason is this site's own promise: *we do not sell you the number — the chain is public and you can compute it yourself. We sell you who it is made of.* What stays paid is exactly that decomposition: which counterparties rated, how many times each, in what facet, on what date and in which transaction — `GET /reputation/wallet/{wallet}`.

Chains where the wallet holds an identity but has **no** ratings are listed with `final_score: null`. That is a fact, not a gap: 'registered here and nobody rated it' and 'not here at all' are different answers and must not collapse into the same empty row.

**Where these numbers come from, and how old they are.** The identities are read live from the index; the reputation comes from the materialized view named in `source`, which is recomputed after each indexing run. `refreshed_at` is when that last succeeded — and it is `null` when no refresh was ever recorded, never a stand-in timestamp. This matters because the paid decomposition (`GET /reputation/wallet/{wallet}`) reads the live grain: if the two disagree, the gap is the time between `refreshed_at` and now, and you are entitled to know that instead of guessing which number is broken.

get.description:
**The sweep door, free.** Whether a wallet holds any ERC-8004 identity and any reputation, as booleans and counts — sized for checking a thousand addresses before spending a cent on any of them.

**This service does not charge for saying there is nothing.** Every figure here is already free, chain by chain, in `GET /wallets/{wallet}/chains`; this route drops the agent ids and the scores so the answer stays small.

`next` says where to go, and each key appears only when it applies. `next.free` is there when the wallet holds an identity. `next.paid` —the paid decomposition, its price, and a preview of one count and one date— is there **only when an identity has ratings to decompose**. Absent means nothing to buy. The preview is counts and dates: never a value, never an address.

`next.paid.price_usd` comes from the same paywall that charges, but this response is cacheable at the edge for about a minute: **the authoritative price for the call is the `accepts[]` of its own 402**.

The counts come from the materialized view named in `source`, recomputed after each indexing run; `refreshed_at` is when that last succeeded.
